digest.top_line: PMRT nomogram, T1-2N1: high-risk tier (score >18) 5y LRR 2.2% vs 14.9% with PMRT, HR 0.164; no significant LRR difference in low or intermediate tiers.
digest.tldr: A breast-only day of retrospective single-institution series on regional RT decisions. In T1-2N1, risk-stratified selection puts the PMRT LRR benefit in the high-risk tier. For isolated chest wall LRR, whole-chest-wall salvage fields beat small fields (5-yr freedom from re-recurrence 75% vs 36%). Nothing here is randomized, and selection and era confounding limit every read.

sites.intro: Five retrospective series bearing on PMRT selection, SCV field omission after positive SLN, and RT salvage of chest wall recurrence.

studies.name: Close or positive margin after mastectomy and chest wall irradiation
studies.tldr: 8yr cumulative chest wall recurrence 28% age ≤50 vs 0% age >50 (p=0.04) with close/positive margin, T ≤5cm, 0-3 nodes, no PMRT.
details: 📊 8yr cumulative chest wall recurrence, all 34 pts: 18% (5yr 9%)

details.text: 📊 Crude chest wall recurrence by age band

details: 📐 Margin ≤2mm vs 2.1-6mm at 8yr: 24% vs 7%, p=0.36 (not significant)
🔍 Retrospective single-institution series (Fox Chase); 34 of 789 mastectomy pts met criteria

details.text: 🔍 Margin distribution (microscopic, deep margin)

details: 💊 Chemo ± tamoxifen in 67%; tamoxifen alone 21% (CMF, CAF, AC era)
📊 5 of 5 chest wall failures: 1 isolated first failure; 3 associated with distant mets
⚠️ Age confounded with systemic therapy: chemo in 91% of ≤50 vs 25% of >50
⚠️ 5 events total; subgroup p=0.04 rests on 5 vs 0 failures
🔗 Ahlborn and Mentzer series (cited in source) found no significant margin effect, short f/u, crude rates only

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-institution series, 5 events; age subgroup confounded with chemo use (91% vs 25%); no RT comparator arm, so PMRT benefit inferred not measured.
verdict.audience: T ≤5cm, 0-3 positive nodes, close (≤6mm) or positive deep margin, post-MRM

studies.significance: Margin distance itself did not separate risk (≤2mm 24% vs 2.1-6mm 7%, p=0.36); age did, with 28% vs 0% chest wall failure at 8yr. For the PMRT decision in an otherwise low-risk mastectomy pt, this argues for weighting age ≤50 over margin proximity alone, and supports omission in older women with a close margin.
studies.monday_clinic: In a woman ≤50 after MRM with T1-T2 disease, 0-3 positive nodes and a deep margin ≤5mm, this supports discussing chest wall RT despite systemic therapy; it does not support PMRT for the margin alone in women >50, where no chest wall failures occurred in 12-13 pts.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-institution review of 789 mastectomy pts at Fox Chase; 136 (17%) had tumor within 1cm of the deep margin. **34 pts** met criteria and received **no postoperative RT**. Median f/u **59 mo** (range 7-143).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Invasive breast cancer, **clinical T ≤5cm, 0-3 positive nodes**, microscopic deep margin ≤1cm, MRM in all. Median age **43** (29-76); 65% node-negative, 35% 1-3 positive nodes; no deep muscle involvement.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Chemo ± tamoxifen in 23 pts (CMF 12, CAF 10, AC 1); tamoxifen alone in 7. Systemic therapy tracked age: **91%** of women ≤50 got chemo vs **25%** of women >50.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 5 chest wall recurrences, median interval 26 mo. Cumulative incidence **9% at 5yr, 18% at 8yr**. Age ≤50 vs >50: **28% vs 0%** at 8yr (p=0.04); margin ≤2mm vs 2.1-6mm 24% vs 7% (p=0.36). 5yr OS 82%, DFS 74%.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The source cites Ahlborn (margin ≤4mm 5.7% vs >4mm 3%) and Mentzer (≤5mm 11% vs >5mm 3%), neither significant and both crude rates at short f/u. This series adds the age interaction those did not report.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents women after MRM with T ≤5cm, 0-3 positive nodes and a close or positive deep margin, not irradiated. Does not represent T3 or ≥4-node disease, gross muscle involvement, or breast-conserving surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Age band estimates rest on 11-12 pts per group. 19 of 34 margins were not centrally re-reviewed. Systemic therapy is **pre-taxane, pre-HER2-targeted**, so absolute risks likely overstate contemporary failure rates.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The title's claim is really two claims: margin alone does not drive risk, and young age does. The first rests on a non-significant comparison in 34 pts, which is absence of evidence rather than evidence of no effect.

studies.interpretation:
The paper's headline is phrased as a negative (a close or positive margin is not an indication) with a carve-out (except in women 50 or younger), and the two halves deserve different levels of confidence. The carve-out is the positive finding: 28% versus 0% chest wall failure at 8 years, p=0.04. The negative half rests on the observation that margin proximity did not separate risk within the cohort, 24% at ≤2mm versus 7% at 2.1-6mm with p=0.36. That is a large point difference reported as non-significant in a series with five events. Read honestly, margin distance was not shown to matter; it was not shown to be irrelevant either. A reader who takes away "margin doesn't matter" has over-read the data.

The age finding has its own problem, and the authors flag it themselves. Age was tightly coupled to systemic therapy: 91% of women ≤50 received chemotherapy versus 25% of those over 50, and four of the five chest wall failures occurred in chemotherapy-treated patients. With zero events in the older group, no multivariable model can disentangle age from treatment selection or from the biology that prompted chemotherapy in younger women. The authors argue chemotherapy has not been shown to prevent locoregional failure in high-risk mastectomy cohorts, which is a reasonable framing, but the more parsimonious reading is that young age and aggressive features travel together and this series cannot say which carries the risk.

Against the two prior margin series the paper cites, Ahlborn and Mentzer, the direction is consistent: both saw numerically higher local recurrence with close margins, neither significant, both with crude rates over roughly three to four years. Freedman's contribution is longer follow-up with cumulative incidence methods, and the observation that failures accrue late (range out to 127 months), which is exactly why short crude series would underestimate risk. That point about follow-up duration is arguably more durable than the age cutoff itself.

For transfer to current practice, the systemic therapy era matters. Patients received CMF, CAF or AC, without taxanes, HER2-directed therapy or modern endocrine sequencing, and with radiology and pathology standards of the mid-1980s to early 1990s. Contemporary locoregional failure rates after mastectomy are lower across the board, so the 28% figure should be treated as an upper bound for a young, close-margin patient today rather than a working estimate. The relative signal, that younger women carry disproportionate chest wall risk when margins are close, is more likely to survive than the absolute number.

The pathology finding is underappreciated. Gross assessment calling a tumor >5mm but <1cm from the margin missed 43% that were microscopically ≤5mm. If margin status is going to enter a PMRT discussion at all, it has to be a microscopic measurement. What would make this study wrong: a larger contemporary series showing that, after adjusting for grade, receptor status and systemic therapy, young age adds nothing for close-margin, low-nodal-burden disease. Until then, the series is best used as one input that tilts toward chest wall RT in a young woman with a close margin, not as license to omit it in everyone else.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Margin distance did not separate chest wall risk (≤2mm 24% vs 2.1-6mm 7%, p=0.36); age ≤50 did (28% vs 0% at 8yr). Supports considering chest wall RT for a close margin in younger women and questions it in women >50 with T ≤5cm and 0-3 nodes.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Gross deep-margin assessment missed 43% of tumors grossly >5mm but <1cm that were microscopically ≤5mm, while gross ≤5mm calls were 90% specific. Microscopic deep-margin assessment changes who is labelled close, and therefore who is referred for PMRT.

open_questions: Does young age add chest wall risk independent of grade and systemic therapy?
Absolute chest wall risk with modern systemic therapy for close margins
Is PMRT omission safe for close margins in women over 50?

studies.name: Isolated local-regional recurrence after mastectomy: radiotherapeutic management
studies.tldr: 5-yr freedom from chest wall re-recurrence 75% with whole-chest-wall fields vs 36% with small fields (p=0.0001) in 224 pts irradiated for isolated LRR.

details.text: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective, Mallinckrodt, 1964-1986, N=224 treated with curative intent

details: 🔍 Excluded prior postmastectomy RT, failed outside salvage, and clinical/radiographic distant mets

details.text: 🔍 Median f/u 46 mo (range 24-241); survival and failure timed from LRR
📊 Whole cohort 5/10-yr OS 43%/26%; DFS 25%/15%; 5-yr LRC 57%
📊 Outcomes at 5 yr by site of first recurrence
📊 Solitary CW recurrence: freedom from CW re-recurrence by field size

details: 📊 Small-field failures: 33% in-field or marginal, 67% outside the portal but within the CW

details.text: 📊 Failure in an uninvolved site, elective RT vs none

details: 📊 Elective SCV RT: 5-yr survival 53% vs 35% (p=0.03)

details.text: 📐 Dose response by recurrence size
subdetails: Completely excised: control adequate across 4500-7000 cGy
<3 cm: 100% controlled at ≥6000 cGy vs 76% at lower doses
Larger, multiple or diffuse: no dose response; about 50% controlled even to 7000 cGy

details.text: 🔍 Technique: tangents 1.5-6.0 MV to 4500-5000 cGy, 6-12 MeV electron boost; ~90% at 180-200 cGy/d
⚠️ RT-attributable late toxicity
subdetails: Grade 2 in 9%, grade 3 in 1%, no fatal toxicity
Arm edema 8/75 (11%) with elective axillary RT vs 1/109 (1%) without
Pneumonitis 2% (2/92) tangents alone vs 8% (3/37) tangents + parasternal photons
Bone necrosis/fracture in 4 pts, all at >5400 cGy

details: ⚠️ Field size confounded with era: small fields were the early policy, so staging and systemic therapy also changed
⚠️ Small-field group only 14 pts; dose chosen by physician preference, not protocol

details.text: ⚠️ Elective CW p-value reported as .32 in abstract and .33 in discussion
🔗 Toonkel series cited in source: comprehensive nodal RT 54% vs 27% 5-yr survival with CW-only RT (p=0.029)

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective spanning 22 years; field size, dose and elective coverage chosen by era and physician preference, so selection and era effects confound every comparison.
verdict.audience: First isolated LRR after mastectomy, no prior PMRT, no distant mets

studies.significance: Field size carries the strongest signal: 67% of small-field failures landed outside the portal but within the chest wall, supporting whole-CW coverage. Elective SCV RT cut SCV failure 16% to 6%, while elective axillary RT raised arm edema 11% vs 1%, so cover the SCV fossa and leave the uninvolved axilla alone.
studies.monday_clinic: In a first isolated chest wall or nodal recurrence after mastectomy without prior PMRT, this supports whole-chest-wall plus supraclavicular coverage over involved-field RT; it does not extend to re-irradiation after prior PMRT or to the elective uninvolved axilla.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **retrospective** review, Mallinckrodt Institute and affiliates, 1964-1986, **N=224** irradiated with curative intent. Median follow-up **46 mo** (range 24-241); actuarial life-table method.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: First **isolated local-regional recurrence** after radical (34%), modified radical (61%) or total (5%) mastectomy. **Excluded prior postmastectomy RT**, pts failing salvage elsewhere, and clinical or radiographic distant mets. Chest wall alone in 134 (60%).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Entire chest wall via tangents, 1.5-6.0 MV to **4500-5000 cGy** with bolus and a 6-12 MeV electron boost to gross disease; SCV AP field to 4500-5000 cGy at 3 cm. About 90% treated at **180-200 cGy/d**; small 1-2 cm-margin fields used early in the series.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: At recurrence, 49 pts received chemotherapy (most often CMF or CAF) and 69 hormonal therapy, usually tamoxifen. Combined-modality vs RT-alone analysis deferred to a later report.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 5-yr LRC **57%**; whole-CW fields gave **75% vs 36%** 5-yr freedom from CW re-recurrence vs small fields (p=0.0001). For <3 cm lesions, **100%** controlled at ≥6000 cGy vs 76% lower; larger lesions about 50% even at 7000 cGy.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Grade 2 sequelae **9%**, grade 3 **1%**, none fatal. Arm edema **11% vs 1%** with vs without elective axillary RT; pneumonitis higher with a parasternal field (8% vs 2% tangents alone).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Toonkel and co-workers, cited here, found a survival advantage with comprehensive nodal RT, while Deutsch reported the opposite, with that elective-nodal group carrying more extensive disease. Chen saw 27% failure in an uninvolved site after involved-field RT, consistent with this series' case for elective CW and SCV coverage.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with a first isolated chest wall or nodal recurrence after mastectomy who had no prior postmastectomy RT. Does not represent prior-PMRT re-irradiation, pts with distant mets, or recurrences managed with contemporary systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Small-field group was only 14 pts and clustered in the early era, so the field-size effect also captures changes in staging workup and systemic therapy. The elective CW p-value is printed as both .32 and .33, and dose was set by physician preference.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The pattern of failure argues the whole chest wall carries subclinical disease, which favors comprehensive fields over excision alone or small portals. Large, diffuse or combined CW-plus-nodal recurrences stay poorly controlled at any dose, and the authors point to hyperthermia, altered fractionation or systemic combinations in prospective trials.

studies.interpretation:
The durable contribution of this series is its pattern-of-failure argument, not its survival figures. When a solitary chest wall recurrence was treated with a small portal, two thirds of subsequent failures arose outside the field yet within the chest wall. That is a biologic observation about where subclinical disease sits, and it is less sensitive to selection bias than any of the outcome comparisons, because it describes the anatomy of failure within the treated group rather than comparing groups chosen differently. It underpins the whole-chest-wall field that remains the default for an isolated recurrence in an unirradiated chest wall.

The headline field-size comparison deserves less confidence than its p-value suggests. Small fields were used in only 14 pts and belonged to the early part of a 22-year window, before the institution switched policy after seeing frequent relapses. The workup for occult metastases also became more extensive over time, and systemic therapy at recurrence changed. A reader should treat the 75% versus 36% gap as directionally right and its magnitude as unreliable: era, staging intensity and case selection all move with field size here.

The elective coverage findings separate into a credible signal and a weaker one. Supraclavicular failure fell from 16% to 6% with elective SCV RT, a site-specific endpoint where the mechanism is direct. The accompanying survival difference, 53% versus 35%, is harder to accept; elective coverage was more common later in the series and in pts the treating physician judged suitable for larger volumes, and a regional nodal field preventing distant death is a large claim from retrospective data. The elective chest wall result did not reach statistical significance, and the paper reports its p-value inconsistently, but the observation that untreated chest walls kept failing as late as 8 and 11 years while treated ones did not after 3 years is the more informative detail for a reader weighing long-term risk in a pt with a long disease-free interval.

The toxicity data are the most transferable to modern practice. Arm edema concentrated in pts given elective axillary RT, and axillary re-recurrence in an uninvolved axilla was uncommon regardless of treatment, which makes omission of the dissected, uninvolved axilla a defensible position that later practice has largely adopted. The pneumonitis gradient with an added parasternal field reflects 2D technique and would need re-evaluation with CT planning.

The dose findings should be read as a ceiling, not a recipe. Small excised or sub-3 cm lesions were controlled reliably, while large, multiple or diffuse disease sat near 50% control without a dose response. That points away from escalation as the answer for bulky recurrence and toward systemic integration, which this paper explicitly deferred. Later work on chemotherapy after isolated locoregional recurrence, such as CALOR, addressed that question directly, and the modern reader will layer endocrine and HER2-directed therapy onto the volumes this paper defined. What would make this series wrong is a demonstration that, with modern imaging, recurrences selected for small fields were genuinely confined; nothing in these data rules that out, but nothing supports it either.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Two thirds of small-field failures landed outside the portal but within the chest wall, supporting whole-CW coverage. Elective SCV RT cut SCV failure 16% to 6%, while elective axillary RT raised arm edema 11% vs 1%, arguing for SCV coverage and omission of the uninvolved axilla.

open_questions: Elective nodal RT benefit with contemporary systemic therapy
Better local control for large or diffuse chest wall recurrences

studies.name: Nomogram for four or more involved nodes in SLN-positive breast cancer
studies.tldr: AUC 0.83 in derivation and 0.81 in external validation for predicting ≥4 involved nodes after 1-3 positive SLNs, using 7 pathologic factors.
details: 🔍 Retrospective review at 2 academic centers (MGH n=248, BWH n=154), N=402
🔍 Eligibility: clinically node-negative invasive breast cancer, 1-3 H&E-positive SLNs, completion ALND (≥6 nodes)
🔍 No neoadjuvant systemic therapy; keratin-only SLN deposits excluded
📊 ≥4 involved nodes in 87 pts per the abstract; the results text says 81

details.text: 📊 Nomogram score (Fig 2), with likelihood read off the total-score scale
subdetails: +11 each for LVSI, lobular histology, extranodal extension
+16 if the largest SLN metastasis is a macrometastasis (>2 mm)

details: 📐 Derivation AUC 0.83 (n=344 with all 7 factors known)
📐 External validation AUC 0.81 (n=206, Sibley community hospital)
📐 At a 5% cutoff: NPV 94.7%, sensitivity 97.5%; 118 pts classified ≤5%
⚠️ The stated counts (113/118 and 54/57) don't clearly match the reported NPV and sensitivity
📊 <5% predicted risk: 34% of derivation and 37% of validation pts could skip the SCV/apex field
⚠️ The nomogram underestimated observed ≥4-node cases in the validation set
⚠️ Selection bias: only dissected pts included; 73 trial pts given nodal RT without ALND were excluded
🔗 Chagpar et al built a similar model (1,133 SLN+ pts) without LVSI or SLN metastasis size
⚠️ No regional-failure outcomes: tangent-only RT in the low-risk group was not tested

verdict.rationale: Retrospective model built on dissected pts with one small external validation. It predicts nodal burden, not regional recurrence after RT field reduction; the omission hypothesis was never tested.
verdict.audience: cN0 invasive breast, 1-3 H&E-positive SLNs, no neoadjuvant therapy

studies.significance: The RT question is field design. With a <5% predicted ≥4-node risk as the threshold, 34% of the derivation and 37% of the validation cohort were candidates to drop the SCV/apex field. The source ties adding that field to lymphedema rising from 2% to 8% to approximately 9% to 24%. The case for omission rests on high tangents covering most of levels I-II.
studies.monday_clinic: In cN0 pts with 1-3 H&E-positive SLNs and no completion ALND, a low predicted ≥4-node risk informs whether to add an SCV/apex field. It does not extend to post-neoadjuvant pts or keratin-only SLN deposits.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** two-center review (MGH n=248, BWH n=154), N=402. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression, forward stepwise selection. External validation in a **separate, previously published community-hospital set of 206 pts**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Clinically node-negative** invasive breast cancer with **1-3 H&E-positive SLNs** and completion ALND, defined as **≥6 nodes examined**. No neoadjuvant systemic therapy. Mastectomy 46%, breast conservation 53%.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Outcome modeled:** ≥4 involved axillary nodes (SLN plus non-SLN). Model performance was assessed by AUC, Hosmer-Lemeshow, sensitivity and NPV.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Seven independent factors: tumor size, lobular histology, LVSI, ENE, number of positive SLNs, macrometastasis, and number of negative SLNs. **AUC 0.83** in derivation, **0.81** in validation. At a 5% cutoff, **NPV 94.7%** and sensitivity 97.5%.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: The authors' hypothesis is that pts below **5% predicted risk** could be treated with **modified high tangents** instead of comprehensive nodal RT to the SCV fossa and axillary apex. That would have spared **34%** (derivation) and **37%** (validation).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Similar in aim to the MD Anderson mastectomy series, where pts without three risk features had **<2% risk** of ≥4 nodes, and to Chagpar et al's 1,133-pt model. This model adds LVSI and SLN metastasis size. It predates the Z0011 and AMAROS axillary-management era.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents cN0, H&E SLN-positive pts with 1-3 positive SLNs and no neoadjuvant therapy. Does not represent post-neoadjuvant pts, keratin-only SLN deposits, or pts with ≥4 positive SLNs.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The **≥6-node** ALND definition may include axillary samplings. The abstract and results disagree on the count of ≥4-node pts (**87 vs 81**). Validation underestimated observed cases, and the validation set was chosen for availability.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The tool estimates **nodal burden, a surrogate** for the risk of regional failure. Whether tangent-only RT is safe in the low-risk group needs outcome data the paper doesn't have.

studies.interpretation:
This paper belongs to the period when sentinel node biopsy had removed the routine axillary dissection but not the uncertainty it used to settle. The clinical question it answers is narrow: if a woman with one to three positive sentinel nodes does not go on to completion dissection, how likely is it that four or more nodes are involved? That threshold mattered because nodal count drove the decision to treat the supraclavicular fossa and axillary apex. The authors frame the nomogram as a way out of a default many radiation oncologists had settled into: comprehensive nodal RT for every SLN-positive pt, which treats the axilla as if it had never been evaluated.

The model's discrimination is respectable. It held up in a community-hospital set, which is the most useful thing about the validation. But a tool built to predict nodal count is two steps away from the outcome a radiation oncologist actually cares about. The first step is from predicted nodal burden to regional recurrence risk. The second is from recurrence risk to the safety of a reduced field. The paper offers no recurrence data for either. The argument for omitting the third field leans on older reports that supraclavicular failure is rare below four nodes, and the authors themselves concede those reports may undercount failures in that region.

The methodology should temper confidence in three specific ways. Derivation drew only on pts who underwent dissection, so the people the tool is meant for (those who skip dissection) were excluded by design. The ≥6-node cutoff for a real dissection is a pragmatic proxy that could let samplings in. And the abstract and results disagree on how many pts had four or more nodes, while the reported sensitivity and NPV do not line up neatly with the counts given beside them. None of this sinks the model, but it argues for treating the 5% threshold as an approximate cut point rather than a calibrated one, especially since the nomogram underpredicted in the validation set.

The practice context has since shifted. Z0011 and AMAROS reframed axillary management for low-volume SLN disease, and MA.20 and EORTC 22922 reopened the case for regional nodal irradiation in node-positive disease more broadly. A tool that helps de-escalate nodal fields sits awkwardly next to trials that pushed toward treating them. Its lasting value is as one input to individualizing the upper-axilla and supraclavicular field when dissection is omitted, not as a stand-alone license to omit. The decision it informs is field extent. It does not address whether nodal RT is indicated at all, which depends on factors beyond nodal count that the model does not capture.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: This informs the SCV/apex field when ALND is omitted. A <5% predicted ≥4-node risk covered 34% to 37% of pts, and the source ties adding the third field to lymphedema rising from 2% to 8% to approximately 9% to 24%. There are no regional-failure data behind the reduced field.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: The model estimates residual nodal burden after 1-3 positive SLNs from pathology, including the number of negative SLNs and SLN metastasis size, without completion dissection. It informs whether completion ALND would change staging, but it was derived only in pts who had ALND with ≥6 nodes.

open_questions: Is tangent-only RT safe for regional control in the <5% group?
Does the nomogram stay calibrated in pts who never have completion ALND?
Should field decisions use predicted nodal count at all?

studies.name: Nomogram for locoregional recurrence in T1-2N1 breast cancer (PMRT decision-making)
studies.tldr: High-risk nomogram tier (score >18): PMRT 5y LRR 2.2% vs 14.9%, HR 0.164; no LRR association in low or intermediate tiers.

details.text: 🔍 Retrospective single-institution cohort, N=1141 T1-2N1, mastectomy + ALND, 2001-2012

details: 🔍 518 (45.4%) received PMRT; median f/u 74.9 mo

details.text: 🔍 Nomogram built in 623 unirradiated pts from 5 factors: tumor size, positive nodes, ER, grade, LVI

details: 📐 Bootstrap C index 0.73 (95% CI 0.68-0.78); calibration internal only

details.text: 📊 Decision-tree cutoffs at scores 10 and 18: crude LRR without PMRT 0.8%, 6.1%, 15.9% by tier
📊 PMRT vs no PMRT by nomogram risk tier (5y cumulative incidence, multivariate HR)
📊 LRR events, PMRT vs no PMRT (Fig 3)
🔍 RT: 46-50 Gy/23-25 fx, CT-planned; chest wall + infraclavicular + supraclavicular

details: 🔍 IMN added for central tumors; axilla added for ECE
⚠️ PMRT not randomized: recipients were younger, earlier era, larger tumors, more nodes, higher grade
⚠️ Risk score and cutoffs derived and tested in the same cohort; no external validation
⚠️ Low-risk null rests on 2 LRR events; absence of benefit is underpowered, not demonstrated

🔗 vs EBCTCG 1-3 node pts: control 10-yr LRR 21%, far above this cohort's 6.0% 5-yr unirradiated LRR

verdict.rationale: Retrospective, clinician-allocated PMRT; risk cutoffs data-derived and tested on the same cohort without external validation. Low-risk null rests on 2 events.
verdict.audience: T1-2N1 breast, mastectomy + ALND, no neoadjuvant therapy

studies.significance: The omission case is the low-risk tier: 5y LRR 0.4% without PMRT and 0/160 vs 2/252 events, so any RT gain there is bounded near zero. Benefit concentrates above score 18 (14.9% → 2.2% LRR, 7.0% BCM reduction) with chest wall plus supraclavicular/infraclavicular fields at 46-50 Gy, i.e. standard comprehensive PMRT.
studies.monday_clinic: In T1-2N1 pts after mastectomy and ALND without neoadjuvant therapy, ER-positive, grade I-II, LVI-negative T1 disease with 1-2 nodes, this supports a PMRT omission discussion; it does not address pts after neoadjuvant therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-institution cohort of **1141** consecutive pts treated 2001-2012. Nomogram from Fine and Gray competing-risks regression in **623 unirradiated** pts; risk tiers by decision tree (CHAID); internal bootstrap validation only. Median follow-up **74.9 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **T1-2, 1-3 positive axillary nodes**, mastectomy with negative margin plus ALND (median 17 nodes dissected). Excluded neoadjuvant therapy, synchronous metastases, other malignancy. All received adjuvant chemotherapy, 90.5% anthracycline- or taxane-based; median age 47.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **46-50 Gy in 23-25 fx**, CT-based planning. Fields: ipsilateral chest wall, infraclavicular and supraclavicular; **IMN only for central tumors**, axilla only with ECE.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **LRR** as first event (chest wall or regional nodes), DR and BCM, all as cumulative incidence with death as a competing risk.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Nomogram C index **0.73**. Risk tiers by score: low ≤10 (n=412), intermediate (n=385), high >18 (n=344). PMRT associated with lower LRR, DR and BCM **only in the high-risk tier**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: EBCTCG showed PMRT benefit in 1-3 node pts, but its control 10-yr LRR of **21%** is well above this cohort's 6.0% 5-yr unirradiated rate, which is the gap a risk model tries to exploit. SUPREMO (NCT00966888) is the prospective test of selective PMRT in this setting.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents T1-2N1 breast cancer after mastectomy with negative margins and ALND, no neoadjuvant therapy, all given adjuvant chemotherapy. Does not represent pts after neoadjuvant therapy, or T3-4 or 4+ node disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: PMRT recipients skewed to adverse features, so within-tier comparisons carry residual confounding. Era of **low trastuzumab use (26.2%)** and no capture of nodal size or margin width; a prior 242-pt nomogram (Wadasadawala) used different factors.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The model mostly formalizes features clinicians already weigh (T stage, node count, ER, grade, LVI) into a score. Its value is the low-risk tier's very low baseline LRR, which supports omission, but **the benefit estimates need external validation** before they guide individual decisions.

studies.interpretation:
The useful output of this paper is a prognostic statement, not a treatment-effect estimate. The nomogram is trained on unirradiated pts, so what it quantifies is baseline locoregional risk after mastectomy and ALND, and on that question it is reasonably credible: a C index of 0.73 from five factors that any breast radiation oncologist already weighs. The decision tree then cuts that score into tiers, and the low tier carries a 5-year LRR of 0.4% without PMRT. Whatever the true relative effect of RT, the absolute gain available there is close to nothing, and that holds regardless of whether the PMRT comparison in the paper is confounded.

The treatment-effect half is weaker. PMRT was allocated by clinicians, and the paper itself reports that recipients were younger, larger, more node-positive and higher grade. Adjustment for measured covariates cannot reach what was not recorded, and the authors concede they lacked nodal size and margin width, both of which plausibly drove referral. The high-risk result (LRR 14.9% to 2.2%, BCM 13.3% to 6.3%) is directionally consistent with EBCTCG, which the authors cite as translating a 16.5% local-control gain into a 7.9% breast cancer mortality gain at 20 years. A skeptic would note that here a breast cancer mortality gain of 7.0% is already visible by 5 years, earlier than a pure local-control mechanism would predict, which is the pattern one expects when the treated and untreated groups differ in ways the model did not capture.

The null results in the low and intermediate tiers should be read as underpowered rather than negative. Two LRR events in 252 unirradiated low-risk pts cannot show a benefit, and the authors say as much. That matters most for the intermediate tier, where baseline 5-year LRR is 6.1%: that is not trivial, and this cohort cannot tell a reader whether RT helps there. That tier is where the real disagreement in T1-2N1 PMRT lives.

Transfer to current practice runs in one direction. Every pt here had ALND with a median of 17 nodes removed, adjuvant chemotherapy, no neoadjuvant therapy, and HER2-directed therapy in only a quarter of HER2-positive cases. Modern systemic therapy should push baseline risk down further, which makes the low tier's omission case stronger and the high tier's absolute benefit likely smaller than reported. Pts treated after neoadjuvant therapy are outside the data entirely, as the authors note in pointing to NSABP B-51.

The model would be wrong in a way that matters if external validation shows the high-risk tier was an artifact of fitting cutoffs to this cohort's events, or if SUPREMO finds no meaningful benefit across the 1-3 node population. Until then it is a reasonable way to structure an omission conversation for favorable T1-2N1 disease, not a basis for withholding RT from the intermediate tier.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Low-risk tier baseline 5y LRR is 0.4% with 0/160 vs 2/252 events, bounding any PMRT gain near zero and supporting omission. The high-risk tier (score >18) carries the benefit, 14.9% → 2.2% LRR, with standard chest wall plus supraclavicular/infraclavicular fields at 46-50 Gy.

open_questions: External validation in an independent, contemporary cohort
PMRT benefit in the intermediate-risk tier with adequate events
Role of PMRT after neoadjuvant therapy

studies.name: Chest wall recurrence outcome by initial stage
studies.tldr: 5-yr OS after isolated CWR 79.9% vs 41.9% vs 29.1% (T1-T2N0 vs T1-T2 1-3 N+ vs T3-T4/>4 N+); 1-3 N+ salvage as poor as advanced stage.
details: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective (MD Anderson), CWR evaluated 1988-1998, N=96
🔍 All pts post-mastectomy, no prior PMRT, isolated CWR without distant mets
🔍 Of 155 identified: 25 excluded for distant mets at CWR, 34 for RT to the primary
🔍 Median f/u 41.4 mo from CWR (range 3.3-166.8)

details.text: 🔍 Baseline and salvage treatment by group (Table 1)
📐 Cox MVA for OS after CWR

details: 📊 No XRT for CWR also predicted worse DMFS on MVA: OR 4.024 (1.825-8.874), p=0.001
🔗 Source cites PMRT trials: ~30% → ~10% 10-yr LRR, 9% absolute OS gain
⚠️ Reported as 'OR' from Cox models; these are hazard ratios mislabeled
⚠️ Group 3 5-yr OS is 29.1% in abstract/text but 21.8% in Table 2, which lists 29.1% as 10-yr
⚠️ Univariate pairwise DMFS ORs repeat the OS values exactly (3.516, 5.326, 1.515); likely copy error
⚠️ Group 2 n=20: null 2 vs 3 contrast is underpowered, not evidence of equivalence
⚠️ Group 3 omitted PMRT despite SOC (refusal, physician bias, often unknown): selected cohort
⚠️ Salvage RT dose, fields and technique not reported

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective, n=20 in the key 1-3 N+ group, non-uniform salvage, internal table/text discrepancies; PMRT benefit inferred from salvage outcomes, never tested.
verdict.audience: Post-mastectomy isolated CWR, no prior PMRT, no distant mets

studies.significance: The RT read has two parts. Omitting RT for the CWR carried OS OR 4.524 on MVA, and pts with T1-T2 1-3 N+ disease salvaged no better than T3-T4/>4 N+ (5-yr OS 41.9% vs 29.1%). The PMRT decision in 1-3 N+ therefore rests on preventing CWR, not on rescuing it. Salvage dose and field are not reported.
studies.monday_clinic: In T1-T2 breast cancer with 1-3 positive nodes after mastectomy, this supports counting salvage of a chest wall recurrence as unreliable when weighing PMRT; it does not extend to T1-T2N0 pts, whose 5-yr OS after CWR was 79.9%.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Single-institution retrospective** chart review of pts seen for CWR at MD Anderson 1988-1998. Kaplan-Meier, log-rank and Cox regression; time 0 = CWR diagnosis. Median f/u **41.4 mo** from CWR.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **N=96** post-mastectomy pts with pathologically confirmed CWR, **no prior PMRT**, no distant mets at CWR. Groups: **T1-T2N0 (n=41)**, **T1-T2 with 1-3 N+ (n=20)**, **T3-T4 or >4 N+ (n=35)**. Group 3 had more LVI (62.9%) and neoadjuvant therapy (40.0%).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: XRT was part of CWR salvage in **70.7% / 75.0% / 68.6%** (p=0.879). Of the 29 not irradiated, reasons included refusal (6), progression on systemic therapy (6), no referral (3) and unknown (10). Dose, fractionation and target volume are not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **OS** and **DMFS** from the date of CWR.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 5-yr OS **79.9% vs 41.9% vs 29.1%** (p=0.0001); 5-yr DMFS **75.2% vs 33.6% vs 25.9%**. Group 1 beat Groups 2 and 3, and **Group 2 vs 3 did not differ** (MVA OR 1.544, p=0.330). **No XRT for CWR** independently predicted worse OS (OR 4.524) and DMFS (OR 4.024).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The PMRT trials the authors cite showed ~30% → ~10% 10-yr LRR and a 9% absolute OS gain in high-risk populations, which supports PMRT for T3-T4 or ≥4 N+. This series adds the salvage half of the argument for 1-3 N+, where the authors describe the LRR risk without RT as ~10-15%.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-mastectomy pts with isolated CWR who never received PMRT, treated in a 1988-1998 era. Does not represent pts recurring after PMRT, those with synchronous distant mets, or contemporary systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Cox estimates are labeled 'OR'. Group 3 5-yr OS differs between abstract (29.1%) and Table 2 (21.8%), and the DMFS pairwise ORs duplicate the OS values. The benefit of salvage XRT is confounded by indication: pts progressing on systemic therapy were not irradiated.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: If salvage of a CWR in 1-3 N+ disease is **as poor as in advanced stage**, then the PMRT decision has to rest on prevention, which means the absolute LRR reduction becomes the deciding number. The series cannot say what that reduction is worth in OS. The authors defer that to the randomized Intergroup trial.

studies.interpretation:
The argument this paper makes is indirect but useful. Whether PMRT improves survival for a subgroup depends on three quantities: the baseline locoregional risk, the toxicity of treatment, and how well a recurrence can be salvaged. The third is usually waved away with the assumption that an isolated chest wall recurrence can be treated when it appears. For node-negative disease this series supports that assumption, with 5-yr OS after CWR of 79.9%. For T1-T2 tumors with 1-3 positive nodes it does not: 41.9% at 5 years, statistically indistinguishable from the T3-T4 or >4 node group that has long been irradiated by default. If the comparison holds, a recurrence in the intermediate group is a marker of systemic failure as much as a local event, and the case for PMRT there is about prevention rather than rescue.

The methodology limits how far that can be taken. The key group has 20 pts, so the null contrast between Groups 2 and 3 (OR 1.544, 95% CI 0.645-3.699) is compatible with a meaningful difference in either direction. Calling the two groups equivalent overstates what the confidence interval allows. The cohort is also selected: it contains only pts who recurred, and the advanced-stage pts who skipped PMRT did so for reasons often recorded as refusal, physician bias, or unknown. The arithmetic needs checking too. Cox estimates are labeled odds ratios, the Group 3 5-yr OS reads 29.1% in the abstract but 21.8% in Table 2, and the univariate DMFS pairwise estimates repeat the OS figures to three decimals. None of these overturns the direction, but they argue against quoting the exact magnitudes.

The salvage RT finding needs the most caution. Omitting RT for the CWR carried an OR of 4.524 for death on multivariable analysis, but the reasons RT was withheld include progression on systemic therapy, so the variable partly encodes biology that was already bad. It is reasonable support for irradiating an isolated CWR, which was already standard practice at the institution. It is not a clean estimate of what RT adds. Dose, field design and technique are not reported, so there is no transferable parameter for an RT reader.

The question the authors left to a randomized trial, whether PMRT improves OS in 1-3 node-positive disease, is the one that matters. This series cannot answer it. What it contributes is the reason the question deserves an answer: if salvage is unreliable, even a modest absolute LRR reduction could translate into survival, which fits the authors' note that pts accept treatment for OS gains as small as 1-2%. The paper would be wrong if the poor outcome in Group 2 reflects the era's systemic therapy or chance in a 20-patient group rather than stage biology. Both are plausible, and a reader should treat the result as a prior that tilts the PMRT conversation for this group, not as evidence that settles it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Omitting RT for the CWR carried OS OR 4.524 on MVA, and pts with T1-T2 1-3 N+ disease salvaged no better than T3-T4/>4 N+ (5-yr OS 41.9% vs 29.1%). The PMRT discussion in 1-3 N+ should treat salvage as unreliable. Salvage dose and field are not reported.

open_questions: Does PMRT improve OS in T1-T2 with 1-3 positive nodes?
Does salvage outcome after CWR hold with modern systemic therapy?
Optimal salvage RT dose and field for isolated CWR

papers.title: Nomogram Predicting Locoregional Recurrence to Assist Decision-Making of Postmastectomy Radiation Therapy in Patients With T1-2N1 Breast Cancer
Nomogram for the Prediction of Having Four or More Involved Nodes for Sentinel Lymph Node–Positive Breast Cancer
papers.abstract: Purpose The standard of care for patients with a positive (+) sentinel lymph node (SLN) is axillary dissection; however, for various reasons, some SLN+ patients do not undergo dissection. The purpose of this study was to define possible predictors of having four or more involved nodes to provide information for clinicians and patients making decisions about adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation. Patients and Methods We reviewed the records of 402 patients with invasive breast cancer and one to three involved SLNs who underwent completion axillary dissection at two academic cancer centers. None of these patients received neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Factors associated with having four or more involved axillary nodes (SLNs and non-SLNs) were evaluated by univariate and multivariate logistic regression analysis. Results Eighty-seven patients had four or more positive nodes. On multivariate analysis, having four or more SLNs was associated with tumor histology, primary tumor size, lymphovascular space invasion, extranodal extension, the number of involved SLNs, the number of uninvolved SLNs, and the size of the largest SLN metastasis. A nomogram to predict the probability of having four or more nodes based on patients’ pathologic data was developed from the multivariate logistic regression model. A separate previously published data set of 206 SLN+ patients treated at a community hospital in another city was used to validate this model. Conclusion Patients with a low probability of having four or more nodes can be identified from known pathologic features. The nomogram developed will be helpful to clinicians making adjuvant treatment recommendations.
